# 1.2 - Mean, Median, and Shape {.unnumbered}

A small company puts this in a job ad:

:::{.text-center}
**"Average pay at our company: $\$80{,}000$!"**
:::

Four of the five people there earn less than $\$40{,}000$. How can the ad be true?

In this lesson, you learn two ways to find the center of data: the {{< glink mean >}} and the {{< glink median >}}. You also learn how the {{< glink shape >}} of a graph can make them different.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I find the mean of a data set.
- [ ] I find the median of a data set.
- [ ] I tell if a graph is symmetric, skewed left, or skewed right.
- [ ] I choose the measure that best describes a typical value.
:::

### 1.2.1 - The Mean

The {{< glink mean >}} is also called the **average**.

:::{.remember title="How to Find the Mean"}
1. Add all the values.
2. Divide by how many values there are.
:::

**Example 1:** 2, 3, 8, 3, 4

$$
2 + 3 + 8 + 3 + 4 = 20
$$

There are 5 values.

$$
20 \div 5 = 4
$$

The mean is **4**.

:::{.remember title="The Mean in Symbols"}
$$
\bar{x} = \frac{\Sigma x}{n}
$$

- $\Sigma$ is the Greek capital letter **sigma**. It means **add up**.
- $\Sigma x$ means add up all the values.
- $\bar{x}$ ("x-bar") is the mean.
- $n$ is how many values there are.

For the example: $\Sigma x = 20$ and $n = 5$, so $\bar{x} = \frac{20}{5} = 4$.
:::

***

### 1.2.2 - The Median

The {{< glink median >}} is the **middle** value.

:::{.remember title="How to Find the Median"}
1. Put the values in order.
2. Find the middle value.
:::

**Example 2:** the same data, 2, 3, 8, 3, 4

In order: 2, 3, **3**, 4, 8

The middle value is **3**. So the median is 3.

**Example 3:** an even number of values, 2, 3, 5, 8

There are two numbers in the middle: 3 and 5. The median is the number halfway between them.

$$
(3 + 5) \div 2 = 4
$$

The median is **4**.

:::{.you-try title="Find the mean and the median of 6, 1, 9, 4"}
**Mean:** $6 + 1 + 9 + 4 = 20$. Then $20 \div 4 = 5$. The mean is **5**.

**Median:** In order: 1, **4**, **6**, 9. Then $(4 + 6) \div 2 = 5$. The median is **5**.
:::

:::{.note title="The Mode"}
The {{< glink mode >}} is the value that happens **most often**. In 2, 3, 8, 3, 4, the mode is 3.
:::

***

### 1.2.3 - Shape Changes the Mean

The {{< glink tail >}} is the long, low side of a graph.

:::{.remember title="The Mean Follows the Tail"}
The mean is **pulled toward the tail**. The median is not pulled much.
:::

![](/images/Unit_1/1.2_shapes.svg){width="640px" fig-align="center"}

| Shape | What it looks like | Mean and median |
|---|---|---|
| {{< glink "skewed left" text="Skewed left" >}} | Tail on the left | mean < median |
| {{< glink symmetric text="Symmetric" >}} | Both sides match | mean ≈ median |
| {{< glink "skewed right" text="Skewed right" >}} | Tail on the right | mean > median |

:::{.think title="Why does the job ad say $\$80{,}000$?"}
The pay is 30,000, 32,000, 35,000, 38,000, and 265,000 dollars.

The mean is $400{,}000 \div 5 = 80{,}000$ dollars. The owner's pay is a long tail on the right. It pulls the mean up.

The median is 35,000 dollars. That is a better description of a **typical** worker.
:::

***

### 1.2.4 - Real Example: US Household Income

Most households earn a medium amount. A small number of households earn millions of dollars. That makes a long tail on the right.

![](/images/Unit_1/1.2_income.svg){width="640px" fig-align="center"}

:::{.real-world title="US household income (2024)"}
- Median: about **$\$84{,}000$**
- Mean: about **$\$121{,}000$**

Half of households earn less than the median. **Most households earn less than the mean.**

When you hear "the average household," ask: is that the mean or the median?

*Source: US Census Bureau, Income in the United States: 2024. Median $\$83{,}730$. Mean about $\$121{,}000$.*
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Mean and Median**

1. A student recorded how many hours she slept each night for one week.

   7, 8, 6, 9, 7, 5, 7

   a. Find the mean.

   b. Find the median.

2. Six students timed their walk to the bus stop, in minutes.

   15, 22, 18, 30, 19, 16

   a. Find the mean.

   b. Find the median.

3. This dot plot shows how many books some students read this month.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.2_dot_plot_books.svg){width="320px"}

   a. How many students are in the data?

   b. Find the median.

   c. Find the mean.

4. This histogram shows how many minutes some students take to get to school.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.1_histogram_minutes.svg){width="440px"}

   Which bar holds the median? Explain.

***

**One Big Value**

5. A small company has 5 people. Here is what each person is paid in one year.

   | Person | Pay |
   |---|---:|
   | Worker A | $\$30{,}000$ |
   | Worker B | $\$32{,}000$ |
   | Worker C | $\$35{,}000$ |
   | Worker D | $\$38{,}000$ |
   | Owner | $\$265{,}000$ |

   a. Find the mean pay.

   b. Find the median pay.

   c. The company puts this in a job ad: *"Average pay at our company: $\$80{,}000$!"* Is this true? Is it fair to a person looking for a job? Explain.

   d. Leave out the owner. Find the mean pay of the 4 workers. How much did one person change the mean?

***

**Shape**

6. Look at each histogram. For each one, name the shape. Then tell if the mean is greater than, less than, or about equal to the median.

   ![](/images/Unit_1/1.2_histograms_abc.svg){width="640px"}

7. Guess the shape of each data set: skewed left, symmetric, or skewed right. Explain.

   a. The price of every house sold in Columbia this year.

   b. Scores on a very easy test. Most students score 90 to 100.

   c. The heights of all adult women in Missouri.

8. Look at the US household income graph above.

   a. Why is the mean ($\$121{,}000$) bigger than the median ($\$84{,}000$)?

   b. A news story says, *"The average US household earns $\$121{,}000$."* Is this true? Does it describe a typical household? Explain.

   c. Do more than half of households earn less than $\$121{,}000$? How do you know?
